newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: FEATURE-Bhutto rival sees power within grasp.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Bhutto rival sees power within grasp.

text.p: Former prime minister Nawaz Sharif vows to throw robbers into the river Indus and change the face of Pakistan as he campaigns for next Monday's elections.
Flying from town to town in a chartered helicopter, Sharif, 47, the main rival to ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto, 43, talks tough and oozes confidence that he will regain power.
He scatters promises freely, canvassing votes for the tiger, election symbol of his Pakistan Muslim League (PML) party.
Such symbols are vital in polls in Pakistan, where 38 percent, at most, of its 130 million people are literate.
Supporters of Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP) like to portray the party's arrow symbol as skewering the PML's tiger.
"But the tiger is giving full fight to this arrow," Sharif tells a rally in the capital Islamabad. "If I come to power, young men will not run after jobs, jobs will run after them."
Sharif, scion of a wealthy business family from populous Punjab province, also plucks chords of national pride.
"We will eat dry, plain meals but will not stretch begging hands before anyone," he declares.
PRICE COMPLAINT

The plump, balding Sharif, dons local turbans or hats as the location dictates, and sticks to brief speeches, using anecdotes to show how prices soared as Bhutto's three-year government cut subsidies or levied new taxes to slash the budget deficit.

Bhutto was sacked by President Farooq Leghari on November 5 on disputed charges of corruption and misrule. Sharif, in power for 30 months until July 1993, was fired for similar reasons, but was briefly reinstated by the Supreme Court.
Though the once-hesitant Sharif has grown into a confident orator, he has turned down a challenge to debate the fluent Bhutto, once president of the Oxford Union, on television.
"Prime minister Nawaz Sharif," chant Sharif's supporters as his Russian-built helicopter, hired from state-run Pakistan International Airlines, lands in clouds of dust and dry leaves.
"On becoming prime minister, I will throw robbers and harbourers of criminals into the river Indus," he tells a rally at Sukkur, in Bhutto's southern home province of Sindh.
"We will light candles of joy in the homes of the poor. Very soon we will change the face of Pakistan."
PROTEGE OF ZIA-UL-HAQ
Sharif, one-time protege of late military ruler General Mohammad Zia-ul-Haq, often turns his guns on upstart rival Imran Khan, former cricket hero turned politician.
He paints Imran as an agent of Zionism because of his marriage to Jemima Goldsmith, daughter of wealthy Anglo-French financier Sir James Goldsmith, who is Jewish.

"This tiger is the tiger of the Muslim League and Pakistan," he says, pointing to a huge metal tiger shape with neon lights for stripes. "This is not the symbol of Jews or imperialists. We rest only after defeating Jewish conspiracies.
"My politics is people's politics. I don't have dollars from Jews nor have I covered my face with deception," he says.
Imran denies receiving any money from Jewish interests and has offered to quit politics if anybody proves otherwise.
Victory for Sharif could result in Punjabis occupying the three most powerful posts in Pakistan -- prime minister, president and chief of army staff.
People in the three smaller provinces often complain of Punjabis dominating the bureaucracy and military, saying Punjab gets the lion's share of revenue because of its big population.

Sharif, while denouncing Bhutto, a Sindhi, for playing the "provincial card", tells voters he has the panacea for Pakistan's problems, including indebtedness, unemployment, inflation, lawlessness, injustice and corruption.

"Leave all other tasks on February 3, and, after your dawn prayers, take your identity card, reach the polling station and cast your vote," he asks. "You fulfil your duty and I will be firm on my pledge, God willing."
